title: The Robots are coming for your job, and that's okay - Elmer Thomas and Maria Bermudez
talk_summary: Twilio's small docs team built six single-purpose agents (editor, alt-text, jargon simplifier, SEO metadata, outline builder, Slack triage bot) behind a Next.js UI, each wrapping a custom GPT with a style guide and rubric stored in Airtable. Quality is enforced by a layered gate: linter/CI validation, GitHub PR with codeowner review, and human merge, plus weekly feedback loops to tune prompts.

takeaways.technique: Single-purpose narrow agents instead of one megabot
takeaways.what_they_do: They split work into six small agents each owning one repeatable, rule-based task, rather than one general agent doing everything.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Instead of one megabot, we built six singlepurpose agents behind a simple next.js frontend.

takeaways.technique: Rubric/style guide externalized in Airtable, injected per request
takeaways.what_they_do: The agent's style guide and rubric live in Airtable so humans can edit them without code, and they are baked into each agent call.
takeaways.evidence_quote: The custom GPT is it has our style guide and it has our rubric that is baked in. It's actually retrieved from an air table

takeaways.technique: Layered validation gate: lint/CI + codeowner PR review + human merge
takeaways.what_they_do: Agent output is never trusted directly; it passes linter and CI tests, then a GitHub PR with codeowner review, then a human merges only when correct.
takeaways.evidence_quote: We have a validation layer that includes veil linting and CI/CD tests. The GitHub PR adds codeowner review.

takeaways.technique: Weekly user feedback loop to tune prompts
takeaways.what_they_do: They run weekly (sometimes daily/hourly) PR reviews and Slack feedback loops with PMs and engineers, using that feedback to continuously tune prompts rather than assuming the model stays correct.
takeaways.evidence_quote: These feedback cycles, they let us tune the prompts continuously instead of hoping the model magically stays perfect.

takeaways.technique: Pick repeatable, high-volume, low-creativity tasks first
takeaways.what_they_do: They choose agent candidates by a rule of thumb: repeatable, high volume, low creativity, leaving judgment and clarity to humans.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Rule of thumb, pick tasks that are repeatable, high volume, and low creativity. That's the sweet spot for an AI helper.

takeaways.technique: Per-task model selection with explicit experimentation
takeaways.what_they_do: They tested models and picked the one that consistently applied their style guide for the editor task, showing a loading graphic because it is slower.
takeaways.evidence_quote: We've done a lot of experimentation and figured out this is the best model to consistently apply our style guide and rubric.
